summary: A short 1969 note objecting to very high link numbers in the host-host protocol. The author says their site will build its tables around a smaller limit, and that 64 would certainly be sufficient even if 32 seems more realistic.

eli5.summary: This note says a computer does not need numbers for lots of separate conversations, and suggests keeping the count small so it is easier to build.

questions: link number limit host host protocol
subtitle: Limit link numbers to 63 instead of allowing all 256 values.

tldr.problem: The host-host protocol allowed link numbers from 0 to 255, but hosts needed to maintain tables and manage many simultaneous links.
tldr.mechanism: Propose a practical limit of 63 link numbers, reserving higher numbers for instrumentation purposes. Even 32 might be sufficient for practical use.
tldr.outcome: The proposal set a practical expectation for early network implementations.

today: RFC 25 represents early practical guidance on protocol limits. Later protocols evolved more flexible connection management.

sections.title: Why Limit Link Numbers?
sections.content: RFC 25 proposes that no link number over 63 be used in the host-host protocol. The rationale is twofold: 256 link numbers (0-255) are far more than needed for practical host-to-host communication, and reserving the higher numbers (64-255) for instrumentation and future purposes is prudent design.
sections.eli5: The protocol allowed 256 link numbers, but that is too many for normal use.

sections.title: Practical Limits
sections.content: Most hosts will not need to maintain more than 63 simultaneous connections for normal operation. UCLA implemented its link tables to take advantage of this limitation, which reduces table size and implementation complexity. The RFC notes that 32 link numbers may be even more realistic for many purposes, though 64 is certainly sufficient to cover peak usage.
sections.eli5: UCLA built their system to handle at most 63 links, and that works fine for everything they need to do.

sections.title: Instrumentation and Future Use
sections.content: By suggesting an upper limit of 63, RFC 25 reserves link numbers 64-255 for special purposes such as instrumentation, network monitoring, or future extensions. This gives protocol designers flexibility to add new features without conflicting with the standard connection numbering scheme.
sections.eli5: Keeping higher link numbers in reserve lets network managers and designers add special features later.
